title: Blue Wave Expands: Democrats Secure Historic Midterm Control as GOP Rebounds from Election Fallout
snippet: Democrats celebrate a decisive midterm triumph, gaining control of both houses of Congress and several statehouses while tight races in Alaska, Mississippi, and Colorado remain in the spotlight.
content:
WASHINGTON — Democrats are continuing to savor a historic midterm performance after routing Republican candidates across the nation to seize control of the U.S. House of Representatives, the U.S. Senate, and crucial state leadership roles.

Congress Shifts Blue as Key Contests Hang in the Balance

In the Senate, Democrats expanded their footprint by flipping seven seats, bringing their total to 54 compared to the Republicans' 44. Two remaining seats—tightly contested races in Alaska and Mississippi—have yet to be officially declared.

The shift was equally pronounced in the House, where Democrats held 254 seats to the GOP's 162 as of Saturday morning, well past the 218-seat threshold required for a majority. With 19 races still uncalled, projections suggest the party is on track to secure its largest House majority since 2008. Among the key battles still underway is Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, where incumbent Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert trails Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher by roughly 3,200 votes with 97% of the ballots counted.

A Historic Night for Statehouses and Representation

The election cycle marked several groundbreaking milestones across gubernatorial and legislative contests. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia made history as the first Black woman elected governor in the United States, while Democrat Amy Acton became Ohio's first female governor. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds won his race to become the state's first Black governor-elect. Meanwhile, the Senate welcomed its first Muslim member with the election of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

White House Restructures Amid Foreign Policy Fallout

The election outcome triggered immediate political shockwaves inside the executive branch. President Donald Trump announced a major cabinet shake-up, naming senior advisor Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller stated he was "honored beyond words" to step into the role.

Addressing the election results earlier in the week, President Trump expressed a willingness to collaborate with the incoming Democratic majorities while emphasizing he would readily exercise his veto power. He acknowledged that the ongoing war in Iran negatively impacted Republican candidates but stood firm on his administration's foreign policy stance, stating, "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."

However, Vice President JD Vance offered a starker assessment of the midterm defeat, publicly attributing the party's losses directly to the conflict. In a post on X, Vance wrote, "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. The reason we lost is the war."
